# Configuration reference
Every setting in `ansible/group_vars/all.yml`, with the explanation that accompanies it in the file. Edit that file, then either `make apply` (this machine) or `make image` (a new artifact).

## Workstation Configuration
 This is the file to edit. Everything else in this repo is machinery that
 turns what is declared here into a bootable image.
 Change something, then either:
   make image    -> build a fresh image carrying the change
   make apply    -> converge THIS running machine to it, no reimage needed

### `base_bash_force_color_prompt`

`true`

**Interactive shell defaults**
Applied to Ubuntu's shipped .bashrc, in /etc/skel (so users created later
inherit them) and in workstation_user's home (already populated from skel by
the time this runs). These are shell defaults for the image, distinct from
personal dotfiles -- roles/dotfiles deliberately pulls those at first login
rather than baking them in. If chezmoi is later given .bashrc to manage, it
owns the file and these settings are whatever that repository says.

### `base_shell_aliases`

_(list or block — see the file)_

Aliases for every interactive shell, bash and zsh alike, written as one
managed block so that an entry removed from this list also disappears from
the file. A lineinfile per alias could only ever add one; nothing would
retract it. bash gets the block in both .bashrc files above; zsh gets it in
/etc/zsh/zshrc, which every interactive zsh reads before ~/.zshrc -- so a
personal ~/.zshrc (chezmoi's to own) can still override any of these.

### `base_fastfetch_on_login`

`true`

Print system info at login. This installs /etc/profile.d rather than appending
to .bashrc, so it fires for login shells -- a TTY, ssh, `bash -l` -- and not
for every terminal tab. Worth knowing on the desktop: GNOME Terminal opens
non-login shells by default, so the banner shows up over ssh rather than in
each new tab. The sysinfo alias above covers that case.

### `desktop_info_enabled`

`true`

**Hostname and IP on the desktop**
Which machine am I on, answered without opening a terminal. The text is
stamped onto the wallpaper rather than drawn by a desktop widget, which is
how Sysinternals BGInfo has always done it on Windows and how BGINFO4X and
lbginfo do it on Linux.
Not conky, though this repo already installs it: conky is an X11 application
and this desktop is GNOME on Wayland, where it has open upstream bugs -- the
window not appearing, right-alignment failing, own_window_type=desktop
vanishing when the desktop is clicked. Not a GNOME Shell extension either:
extensions break on every GNOME major version, and a wallpaper does not.
desktop_info_base_wallpaper must stay a PRISTINE source image. The generated
file is written elsewhere and set as the wallpaper; stamping the current
wallpaper instead would re-stamp its own output and the text would compound
on every refresh.

### `desktop_info_base_wallpaper`

`/usr/share/backgrounds/warty-final-ubuntu.png`

### `base_apt_retries`

`3`

How many times apt retries an individual failed download. Ubuntu ships no
default, which means zero: one refused connection or DNS blip anywhere in
sources.list.d fails the whole `apt-get update`, and with it `make apply`.

### `base_bash_histsize`

`50000`

### `base_bash_histfilesize`

`50000`

### `workstation_claude_desktop_enabled`

`true`

Claude Desktop. Linux support is beta (Ubuntu 22.04+/Debian 12+, amd64/arm64).

### `workstation_claude_code_enabled`

`true`

Claude Code, the terminal agent. Installed from Anthropic's signed apt
repository rather than the `curl | bash` native installer: that installer
puts the binary in ONE user's ~/.local/bin and self-updates in the
background, which is the wrong shape for an image flashed onto many machines
and used by whoever logs in. The package is system-wide and updates with the
rest of the system.

### `workstation_gh_enabled`

`true`

GitHub CLI, from GitHub's own repository rather than the Ubuntu archive.
The archive carries 2.46.0 against upstream 2.99.0 -- 53 minor versions --
and gh gains subcommands and flags often enough that scripting against the
archive build means checking what exists in it first.

`true`

`true`

### `workstation_balena_etcher_enabled`

`true`

BalenaEtcher and Nimbalyst have no apt repository; both are pinned
downloads, declared in pinned_downloads below with their versions.

### `apps_apt_repos`

_(list or block — see the file)_

**APT: third-party repositories**
Each entry adds a signed keyring and a sources.list.d entry, then installs its
packages from it. roles/apt_repos does the work and checks every entry before
touching anything, so a missing or misspelt field fails the run up front.
- `name`: the entry's name. Our source file is a deb822
  sources.list.d/workstation-<name>.sources, and the keyring defaults to
  /etc/apt/keyrings/<name>.gpg. A one-line <name>.list, which older
  versions wrote, is removed -- except under `vendor_sources`, below.
- `enabled`: optional feature switch.
- `key_url`: the vendor's signing key, fetched on every converge so a
  rotated key is picked up.
- `key_path`: where the keyring goes, when the vendor documents a path of
  its own -- see the vendors below for why matching it matters.
- `key_armoured`: install the key as the .asc the vendor publishes, rather
  than dearmoured. Needs `key_path`.
- `repo`: the deb line, as the vendor documents it:
  `deb [options] uri suite [components]`. It is written out as deb822.
  Its signed-by must name the keyring path above; anything else is refused,
  because it fails later as a signature error that reads like a network
  fault.
- `vendor_sources`: the vendor's package writes its own deb822 source at
  sources.list.d/<name>.sources. Our entry then only bootstraps the first
  install, as the one-line <name>.list the vendor's postinst takes over, and
  is removed once theirs exists. Without it the origin stays declared
  twice.
- `vendor_opt_out`: a setting that stops the vendor's package adding an apt
  source of its own, as `file`, `setting` and `value`. Written before the
  package installs, because its postinst reads it.
- `debsig_key_id` and `debsig_policy_url`: a debsig-verify policy, which
  checks the .deb's own signature on top of apt's repository signature.
- `packages`: what to install from it. Never list these in apps_apt_base:
  apt would try to install them before the repository exists.

### `pinned_downloads`

_(list or block — see the file)_

**Pinned downloads**
Software with no apt repository, snap or flatpak, fetched from a release URL
instead. Each entry is pinned by version and checksum: a release URL alone
verifies nothing, and a checksum mismatch fails the download outright rather
than installing something unverified. Bump deliberately, the same way
dev_mise_runtimes is bumped, and check the new pin with
`python3 scripts/verify-repos.py --checksums` before building.
roles/pinned_downloads installs every entry; `make verify-repos` checks every
entry still exists. Adding one here is all either of them needs. Whatever an
entry needs after it installs -- a wrapper, a desktop entry -- stays in the
role that owns that app (roles/apps for both desktop apps).
- `name`: the entry's name, and the deb package or tarball member to install
  unless `package` or `binary` says otherwise.
- `enabled`: optional feature switch, as in apps_apt_repos.
- `kind`: `deb` installs with apt, so its dependencies resolve, then deletes
  the .deb; the installed version decides whether to fetch it again.
  `tarball` extracts one binary into /usr/local/bin and deletes the archive;
  `<binary> --version` decides. `appimage` is kept at `dest`; the checksum of
  what is already there decides, so a converge never re-fetches it.
- `version`: substituted for every {version} in `url`, so a bump is one line.
- `checksum`: `<algorithm>:<hex>`, as ansible.builtin.get_url takes it.

### `apps_snap`

`[]`

**Snap**
Empty by design. VS Code used to be installed here as a classic snap; it now
comes from Microsoft's apt repository instead (see apps_apt_repos above), and
keeping both would put two independent copies on the image, each with its own
update mechanism and its own ~300MB.

**Flatpak (flathub)**

### `dev_mise_enabled`

`true`

**Language runtimes, via mise**
mise installs per-user toolchains without polluting the system, and pins
versions in one place. Set to {} to skip.

### `dev_mise_runtimes`

_(list or block — see the file)_

### `dev_mise_install_runtimes`

`true`

Whether to download the runtimes above during a converge, as opposed to just
declaring them. Separated because they are different kinds of thing: the
declaration is configuration this repo owns, the download is several hundred
megabytes pulled from four upstreams that can be slow or briefly broken for
reasons that say nothing about whether this config is right.
CI sets this false. Its apply job exists to prove the playbook converges and
settles, and it was instead spending most of its runtime fetching toolchains
and then failing on `mise install core:python` with a filesystem permission
error specific to the runner image -- a red build that told you nothing.
Left true everywhere else, so a real converge still installs them.

## Dotfiles
 Managed with chezmoi. The image ships the chezmoi binary only -- the repo
 is pulled on first login, so nothing personal is baked into a flashable
 artifact and the same image is safe to share or re-flash anywhere.

`true`

### `desktop_autologin`

`false`

Automatic login. Convenient on a personal laptop, weak on a stolen one.

### `desktop_wireshark_capture_as_user`

`true`

Let the workstation user capture packets without sudo.
wireshark-common asks this via debconf and defaults to FALSE, so an
unattended install produces a Wireshark that cannot capture as your user --
and no 'wireshark' group to join, because postinst only creates that group
when this is enabled. Setting it preseeds the answer and adds the user to
the group.
The tradeoff, in Debian's own words: dumpcap becomes setuid/setcap, which
"may be a security risk". It is still the option Debian recommends over
running the whole GUI as root. Set false to ship the stock behaviour, where
capture requires elevation.
